system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2173-11-24 10:30:00 to 2173-11-28 15:47:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for acute abdominal pain in the epigastric and right upper quadrant, distinct from her chronic G-tube site pain and suggestive of a recurrent marginal ulcer. She had run out of oxycodone and found minimal relief with acetaminophen. An ultrasound ruled out cholecystitis, and labs showed transient leukocytosis and elevated lactate, both resolving without signs of infection. She was managed with bowel rest, IV fluids, IV pantoprazole, and later sucralfate, with significant improvement in pain. She resumed tube feeds and oral intake, remained stable, and was discharged home with a plan to continue acid suppression and sucralfate, along with scheduled G-tube revision surgery. Discharge instructions emphasized medication adherence, avoidance of NSAIDs, and monitoring for warning symptoms.

Date of Birth:  ___             Sex:   F
 
Service: SURGERY

NSAIDS (Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drug) / aspirin
 
Attending: ___.
 
Chief Complaint:
g-tube pain
 
Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure:
___ - open gastrostomy tube replacement (Dr. ___

 
History of Present Illness:
The patient is a ___ woman with history
of gastric bypass with problems with hypoglycemia
necessitating round-the-clock tube feeds.  She had a
gastrostomy tube placed in her remnant stomach but,
unfortunately, at some point, had a mechanical pulling of the
tube and subsequent pain which never seemed to resolve
despite various machinations.  We had discussed the options
of re-siting the tube versus simultaneous revisional surgery.
She did contemplate partial pancreatectomy or pancreatectomy
as well as revision of the gastric bypass itself but decided
against these in favor of gastrostomy tube re-siting alone.
She understood potential risks as well as the expected
outcomes and wished to proceed.

 
Past Medical History:
1.  Obstructive sleep apnea, resolved.  
2.  Gastroesophageal reflux, resolved.  
3.  History of polycystic ovary disease.  
4.  History of fatty liver.  
5.  History of gastrojejunal anastomotic ulcer.  
6.  History of C. difficile colitis, ___.  
7.  Depression and anxiety.  
8.  Post-gastric bypass hypoglycemia.  
9.  Breath test positivity for bacterial overgrowth, ___.  
10. MRSA positivity.  

Past Surgical History:  
1.  Right carpal tunnel surgery in ___.  
2.  Right shoulder surgery in ___.  
3.  Tubal ligation in ___.  
4.  Laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass in ___.  
5.  Right internal jugular Hickman placed ___, status 
post removal.  
6.  Appendectomy.
7.  Laparoscopic gastrostomy tube in ___, status post removal.
8.  Interventional placed gastrostomy tube inadvertently placed 
in the Roux limb in ___, status post removal.
9.  Laparoscopic converted to open gastrostomy tube placement in 
___. Currently, tube is ___ MIC gastrostomy 
tube, 20 ___ with a ___ mL balloon.
10. Wound drainage and removal of foreign body (suture) from  
abdominal wall incision in ___.

___

Her family history is remarkable for obesity and CAD.

RRR

surgical incision. Wounds c/d/i without exudative drainage or 
impending dehiscence. 
Extremities WWP, no edema
G-tube in place and functioning appropriately
 
Pertinent Results:
MRSA SCREEN (Final ___:    No MRSA isolated. 

 
Brief Hospital Course:
The patient presented for surgery on ___. Pt was evaluated by 
anaesthesia and taken to the operating room for open gastrostomy 
tube removal and placement of new gastrostomy tube. There were 
no adverse events in the operating room; please see the 
operative note for details. 
Pt was extubated, taken to the PACU until stable, then 
transferred to the ward for observation. 

Neuro: The patient was alert and oriented throughout 
hospitalization; pain was initially managed with a PCA and then 
transitioned to dilaudid tablet given via Gtube.
CV: The patient remained stable from a cardiovascular 
standpoint; vital signs were routinely monitored.
Pulmonary: The patient remained stable from a pulmonary 
standpoint; vital signs were routinely monitored. Good pulmonary

GI/GU/FEN: Patient was initially NPO after the procedure and we 
began continuous tube feeds via her new g-tube on POD 2, and 
ramped up to her previous rate of 65cc/h which she tolerated 
well. 
ID: The patient remained afebrile for the duration of her 
hospital course
HEME: The patient's blood counts were closely watched for signs 
of bleeding, of which there were none.
Prophylaxis: The patient received subcutaneous heparin and ___ 
dyne boots were used during this stay and she was encouraged to 
get up and ambulate as early as possible.

At the time of discharge, the patient was doing well, afebrile 
with stable vital signs.  The patient was tolerating water PO 
and her home course of tube feeds, ambulating, voiding without 
assistance, and pain was well controlled.  The patient received 
discharge teaching and follow-up instructions with understanding 
verbalized and agreement with the discharge plan. ___ will be 
visiting daily to provide dressing changes. 

 
Medications on Admission:
1. Fluoxetine 20 mg PO TID 
2. Rifaximin 550 mg PO/NG TID 
3. Zolpidem Tartrate 5 mg PO QHS

9. Nutrihep (nut.tx.impaired hepatic fxn) 0.04-1.5 gram-kcal/mL 
G-tube continuous 
50cc/hr continuous. 5 cans per day (1800kcal per day).

 
Discharge Medications:

2. Bisacodyl ___AILY:PRN constipation 
3. Acetaminophen (Liquid) 650 mg PO Q6H 
4. HYDROmorphone (Dilaudid) ___ mg NG Q3H:PRN moderate to severe 
pain 
RX *hydromorphone [Dilaudid] 2 mg 1 - 2 tablet(s) by mouth Every 
___ hours Disp #*100 Tablet Refills:*0

 
Discharge Disposition:
Home With Service
 
Facility:
___
 
Discharge Diagnosis:
G-tube pain

 
Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Clear and coherent.
Level of Consciousness: Alert and interactive.
Activity Status: Ambulatory - Independent.

 
Discharge Instructions:
Discharge Instructions: Please call your surgeon or return to 
the emergency department if you develop a fever greater than 
101.5, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe abdominal pain, 
pain unrelieved by your pain medication, severe nausea or 
vomiting, severe abdominal bloating, inability to eat or drink, 
foul smelling or colorful drainage from your incisions, redness 
or swelling around your incisions, or any other symptoms which 
are concerning to you.

Diet: You may drink water, but do not take anything else by 
mouth. Continue tube feeds via your new G-tube at your previous 
continuous rate 65ml/hr. 

Medication Instructions:
Resume your home medications, CRUSH ALL PILLS and administer via 
G-tube.
You will be starting some new medications:
1.  You are being discharged on medications to treat the pain 
from your operation. These medications will make you drowsy and 
impair your ability to drive a motor vehicle or operate 
machinery safely. You MUST refrain from such activities while 
taking these medications.
2. You should take a stool softener, Colace, twice daily for 
constipation as needed, or until you resume a normal bowel 
pattern.
3. You must not use NSAIDS (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory 
drugs) Examples are Ibuprofen, Motrin, Aleve, Nuprin and 
Naproxen. These agents will cause bleeding and ulcers in your 
digestive system.

Activity:
No heavy lifting of items ___ pounds for 6 weeks. You may 
resume moderate exercise at your discretion, no abdominal 
exercises.

Wound Care:
You may shower, no tub baths or swimming. 
You will have nurses to provide dressing changes for your wounds 
aily. 
Please provide routine G-tube maintenance as before. 

Please call the doctor if you have increased pain, swelling, 
redness, or drainage from the incision sites. 

 
Followup Instructions:
___

diagnoses.long_title: Other specified procedures as the cause of abnormal reaction of patient, or of later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of procedure

procedures.long_title: Enteral infusion of concentrated nutritional substances

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. I understand you’ve been having ongoing pain with your G-tube. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been really bothering me. The tube pulled at some point, and the pain never went away. It’s constant around the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had several G-tubes placed before, and this one is in your remnant stomach. We discussed re-siting the tube, and you’ve decided to go ahead with that today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I don’t want more major surgery like revising the bypass or dealing with the pancreas. I just want the tube moved to stop the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. The plan is to remove the current tube and place a new one surgically through an open procedure. It’s low risk, and we expect good relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be asleep? I’m a little nervous about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll be fully under general anesthesia. The anesthesia team will monitor you closely the whole time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s good to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just updating you — you’ve just come out of surgery. The open G-tube replacement went smoothly. No complications. You’re in the recovery area now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, already? I didn’t feel a thing. Is the new tube in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the new tube is securely placed in a better location. You’ll stay on pain medication through the tube for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt when I wake up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have some discomfort, but we’re using a PCA pump at first, then switch to Dilaudid tablets through the tube. Pain should be well controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain now? On a scale of 1 to 10?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe a 5. It’s sore, but not sharp. Better than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That’s expected. You’re doing well — heart rate and breathing are stable. We’ll keep watching you tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I drink water yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. You’ll stay NPO tonight. We’ll start tube feeds tomorrow once we’re sure everything is healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs look good — no signs of infection or bleeding. We’re going to start your tube feeds today at a low rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I was worried about not eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re getting nutrition through the new tube. We’ll ramp up slowly to your usual 65 mL/hour. You’ll stay on Dilaudid for pain as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds? Like fluoxetine and pantoprazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll crush all your pills and give them through the G-tube once you’re tolerating feeds. No NSAIDs — you’re allergic, remember?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, no ibuprofen. I’ll stick to acetaminophen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MRSA screen came back — no MRSA detected. That’s excellent. Means lower infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had it before, so I was worried. Good to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Pain is down, you’re tolerating full feeds at 65 mL/hour, and you walked in the hall this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain is maybe a 2 now. And I feel stronger walking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll keep encouraging movement to prevent clots. You’re on heparin shots and compression boots for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the wound healing okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the incision is clean, no redness or drainage. You’ll have a nurse come daily to change the dressing at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another good night. You’re afebrile, pain is controlled, and you’re passing gas — all signs your gut is working normally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have a little water by mouth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll let you sip water. But keep all nutrition through the tube. No solid food by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my meds — I need to crush them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Crush all pills and mix with water before flushing through the tube. That’s critical.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’re stable, ambulating, and tolerating everything well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you get a fever over 101.5, severe pain, redness or pus from the wound, or can’t keep feeds running.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain meds? I have the Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll get Dilaudid for breakthrough pain. It can make you drowsy, so no driving or heavy lifting over 10 pounds for six weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll have help at home. The nurse will come daily?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a nurse will visit daily for dressing changes. Keep the site clean and dry. You can shower, but no baths or swimming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Final check — you’re afebrile, pain is mild, and you’re eating and drinking small amounts safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Discharge meds include acetaminophen, Dilaudid, and stool softeners for constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take Colace twice a day, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and bisacodyl if needed. Keep up the fluids and movement. Follow up with your surgeon in one week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no NSAIDs — I remember.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ve got it. We’ll get the discharge papers ready. You should be home within a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — you understand to crush all pills and give via G-tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll crush them and flush well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And if the tube clogs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Flush with warm water, and if it doesn’t clear, call the nurse or doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set. We’re discharging you with home health support. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I’m so glad the pain is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — your tube feeds should stay at 65 mL/hour continuously. Don’t adjust the rate unless instructed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Nutrihep at 65 mL/hour, same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. And keep taking pantoprazole and rifaximin as prescribed — they help with stomach acid and gut bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t forget. I’ve been on them a long time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Also, your depression and anxiety meds — fluoxetine and zolpidem — keep those consistent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I take fluoxetine three times a day and zolpidem at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. And clonidine patch once a week. All these go through the G-tube, crushed or dissolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure my caregiver knows the routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’re well prepared. We’ll see you in follow-up, but call sooner if anything concerns you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for fixing the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, and we’ll check in soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for chronic G-tube site pain due to mechanical pulling of the tube, which failed to resolve with prior interventions. She underwent an open gastrostomy tube replacement without complications. Postoperatively, she remained stable, afebrile, and alert, with good pain control managed initially with PCA and transitioned to oral Dilaudid via G-tube. Tube feeds were restarted on postoperative day 2 and advanced to her prior rate of 65 mL/hour, which she tolerated well. She resumed sipping water, ambulated early, and had no signs of infection or bleeding. A MRSA screen was negative. She was discharged home with home health services for wound care, instructions to crush all medications and administer via G-tube, and clear guidance on activity restrictions, diet, and warning signs. Follow-up was arranged with her surgeon.
